items.summary: Judicial proceedings across subordinate courts in Maharashtra faced severe disruptions as approximately 34,000 court employees began their indefinite strike from Tuesday. Protesting staffers staged demonstrations outside several civil and sessions courts outside court complexes. The employees are protesting the State government's failure to implement a proposed wage increment based on the principle of "equal pay for equal work." As per a notice issued to the Principal Judge of the City Civil Court of Mumbai on November 6, the strike has been jointly called by the Maharashtra State Court Employees Sanghatana (Class-C), the Maharashtra State Judicial Stenographers Association, the State Judicial Bailiffs Employees Sanghantana, and the Class-D Employees Sanghatana. Union representatives have expressed deep frustration over the failure to implement this proposal. They highlighted that despite a lapse of nearly 20 to 21 months since the High Court's formal recommendation, the State government has failed to take any concrete decision in the matter. Employees had previously registered their dissent by participating in black ribbon protests on September 16, as well as on October 16 and 17, 2026. items.title: Madras High Court strikes down ban on transport of stone and minerals from Tamil Nadu to other States
items.summary: The Madras High Court on Tuesday struck down a Tamil Nadu (TN) government rule which had empowered authorities to ban the transportation of rough stone and other minerals from TN to neighbouring States [Madhu Premnath Vs State]. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G Arul Murugan declared Rule 3-A of the Tamil Nadu Prevention of Illegal Mining, Transportation and Storage of Minerals and Mineral Dealers' Rules, 2011 unconstitutional and violative of the constitutional guarantee of free trade. It also quashed a July 27 government order imposing a three-month ban on transporting rough stone and aggregates outside Tamil Nadu. The Court held that the State could not invoke provisions intended to prevent illegal mining to restrict the transportation and sale of minerals that had been lawfully excavated. " Any measure of the State to ban transport of mineral to other States or restrict sales except as provided under Part XIII of the Constitution of India, is unconstitutional and would also traverse beyond the legislative competence ," the Court said. The provision empowered the Director of Geology and Mining to regulate the transportation of rough stone, boulders, M-sand, metal jelly and other construction materials to other States, including by imposing temporary bans to ensure adequate domestic supply. Acting under the provision, the Director imposed a three-month ban on July 27, while exempting Puducherry and Karaikal. The petitioners argued that Sections 15 and 23-C of the MMDR Act did not authorise the State to regulate the sale or transportation of minerals after they had been lawfully excavated and the prescribed royalty paid. They also contended that the restriction violated Article 301 of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of trade and commerce throughout India. The State defended the rule, arguing that the government was empowered to regulate mineral transportation under Section 23-C of the MMDR Act. items.title: Palathayi sexual assault: Supreme Court seeks ex-BJP leader's response to plea challenging suspension of his jail sentence
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice on the Kerala government's plea challenging the suspension of the life sentence imposed on former BJP leader and school teacher K Padmarajan in the Palathayi sexual assault case [ State of Kerala v. Padmarajan @ Pappan Mash and Anr. ] . The State government has challenged the Kerala High Court's August 20, 2026 decision to suspend Padmarajan's sentence and grant him interim bail while it considers his appeal against the trial court verdict convicting him in the case. A Bench of Justices MM Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale today issued notice in the matter, thereby seeking Padmarajan's response in the matter. The case will be heard next on January 7, 2027. Justice M.M. Sundresh and Justice Prasanna B. Varale The case arose from allegations that Padmarajan, a school teacher in Kannur district, sexually assaulted a 10-year-old student. A criminal case was registered on March 17, 2020. On November 14, 2025, a special court in Thalassery convicted him under Sections 376(2)(f) (rape by a person in a position of trust or authority), 376AB (rape of a girl below 12 years of age) and 354B (assault or use of criminal force with intent to disrobe) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). He was also convicted under Sections 5(f), 5(l) and 5(m), read with Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, which deal with aggravated penetrative sexual assault and its punishment. The trial court sentenced him to imprisonment for the remainder of his natural life and imposed a fine of ₹1 lakh. He was also sentenced to 20 years' rigorous imprisonment under the POCSO Act. Padmarajan challenged his conviction before the Kerala High Court and sought suspension of his sentence while his appeal was pending. In August, the High Court suspended his sentence and granted him bail. The High Court observed that Padmarajan had made out an arguable case and that there appeared to be some infirmity in the conviction. It pointed to inconsistencies in the evidence, including the child's testimony and medical evidence, as well as differing conclusions reached by investigating agencies. The Kerala government subsequently moved the Supreme Court, seeking to set aside the High Court's order suspending his sentence. The Supreme Court issued notice on the State government's plea today. items.title: Rasna exits insolvency after three years as NCLT approves settlement with creditor
items.summary: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), Ahmedabad Bench on Tuesday allowed an application seeking withdrawal of the corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) against popular beverage concentrate manufacturer Rasna Private Limited, following a settlement between the company and its operational creditor, Bharat Road Carrier Private Limited. A coram of Judicial Member Shammi Khan and Technical Member Sanjeev Sharma orally pronounced the decision today. Interim resolution professional (IRP) Ravindra Kumar Goyal filed the withdrawal application under Section 12A read with Section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. Section 12A of the IBC allows the party that initiated insolvency proceedings to seek withdrawal of the application after it has been admitted, subject to approval by the committee of creditors (CoC) with 90% voting share and compliance with the prescribed procedure. Section 60(5) of the IBC empowers the NCLT to dispose of any application or proceeding by or against the corporate debtor. Rasna had been undergoing insolvency proceedings for over three years, after the NCLT admitted the insolvency petition on September 1, 2023. The proceedings began with Bharat Road Carrier approaching the NCLT in April 2019, alleging that Rasna had failed to pay operational dues of ₹71,27,442, plus interest. The dispute arose from transportation services provided by Bharat Road Carrier to Rasna between April 2017 and August 2018, for which the former company had raised multiple invoices. A demand notice under Section 8 of the IBC was also issued to Rasna in August 2018. Rasna pointed out that it had filed a civil suit seeking damages of ₹1.25 crore against Bharat Road Carrier before the commercial court at Ahmedabad in November 2018. The NCLT, while admitting the insolvency petition, noted that Rasna had filed the civil suit after receiving the payment demand notice. The Tribunal had held that Bharat Road Carrier had established the existence of default exceeding the applicable threshold and admitted the insolvency petition against Rasna. After Rasna and Bharat Road Carrier reached a settlement, the IRP approached the Tribunal to withdraw the insolvency proceedings. The Bench allowed the application today. The written order is awaited.

items.title: Karnataka reconstitutes lawyers' panel to conduct sensitive, communal cases from Mangaluru, Dakshina Kannada
items.summary: The Karnataka government recently reconstituted lawyers' panels tasked with handling sensitive and communal cases arising within the jurisdiction of Mangaluru City Police Commissionerate and Dakshina Kannada District Police Unit before the Karnataka High Court. The Home Department issued two orders on November 7, superseding an earlier order dated July 3, 2025, which had constituted the panels. The decision to reconstitute the panels was taken following a request from the Advocate General's Office, which pointed out that some of the law officers appointed under the earlier panels were no longer working in the office. This had affected the effective conduct of cases before the High Court. The government, after consultation with the Advocate General for Karnataka, decided to reconstitute the panels to ensure effective representation in all sensitive and communal cases arising within the respective police jurisdictions. The following seven law officers have been appointed to handle cases arising within the jurisdiction of Mangaluru City Police Commissionerate: 1. SA Ahmed – Additional Advocate General 2. Shahulla Hameed – Additional Advocate General 3. Rashmi Jadhav – Additional State Public Prosecutor 4. Mohd. Ayub Ali – Additional State Public Prosecutor 5. Mahesh P – High Court Government Pleader The same seven-member panel will handle cases arising within the jurisdiction of Dakshina Kannada District Police Unit. The orders further clarify that the law officers may take assistance from the concerned High Court Government Pleader in conducting these matters. items.title: Former Kerala High Court judge's wife killed after being hit by truck
items.summary: NP Vijayalakshmi, wife of former Kerala High Court Justice PR Raman, breathed her last on Monday after being hit by a concrete mixer truck while crossing a road in Kochi. According to reports , Vijayalakshmi, aged 72, was a resident of Kadavanthra in Ernakulam. She was attempting to cross a road near Kadavanthra signal Junction around 6 PM when the accident occurred. The truck driver, who was waiting for the traffic signal, moved the vehicle forward when the signal turned green. The truck then hit Vijayalakshmi, causing fatal injuries. The Kadavanthra Police which is investigating the circumstances surrounding the accident, has taken the driver into custody and seized the truck. This tragic incident comes amid continuing concerns over road safety in Kochi, where accidents involving heavy vehicles and pedestrians have been recurring with increaing frequency.

items.title: KIIT School of Law organises international conference on the contribution of ICJ towards World Peace
items.summary: Kalinga Institute of Industrial Technology (KIIT) School of Law recently organised an International Law Conference on the theme “Contribution of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) towards World Peace.” The conference featured the participation of three Judges of the International Court of Justice (ICJ): Judge Yuji Iwasawa, President of the ICJ ; Judge Leonardo Nemer Caldeira Brant; and Judge Bogdan-Lucian Aurescu . The occasion was graced by Prof (Dr) Achyuta Samanta , Founder – KIIT, KISS & KIMS; Ashok Kumar Parija , Chancellor; Prof (Dr) Saranjit Singh , Vice-Chancellor; Prof (Dr) NL Mitra , Professor Emeritus; Prof (Dr) Jyana Ranjan Mohanty , Pro Vice-Chancellor-cum-Registrar; and Prof (Dr) KD Raju , Pro Vice-Chancellor, KIIT-DU. The conference brought together eminent legal experts, academicians, jurists and international law practitioners to deliberate on the role of the International Court of Justice in maintaining international peace, resolving disputes between nations and strengthening the international legal order. The deliberations explored the ICJ's role in advancing international justice, promoting the peaceful settlement of international disputes, upholding the principles of international law and strengthening global peace. The discussions also highlighted the importance of international cooperation, respect for the rule of law and the need to reinforce the global judicial framework. The interaction with the ICJ Judges offered a valuable academic experience for students and faculty members, providing them with an opportunity to gain insights into the functioning of the world's principal judicial organ and contemporary challenges in international law.

items.summary: In an unusual administrative move, a part-heard Supreme Court case concerning a nationwide audit of private universities has been reassigned from a Bench led by Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah to a newly constituted three-judge Bench headed by Justice Vikram Nath [Ayesha Jain v. Amity University Noida & Ors]. According to the Supreme Court's case status, the case, which had been regularly heard as a part-heard matter by Justices Amanullah and NV Anjaria until October, will now come up on November 19 before a Bench comprising Justices Nath, R Mahadevan and Aparesh Kumar Singh . No reasons have been disclosed on the judicial record for the sudden change of bench just days ahead of the scheduled hearing. Justice Vikram Nath, Justice R Mahadevan and Justice Aparesh Kumar Singh The development is particularly notable given how aggressively the previous bench had expanded and monitored the present proceedings over the past year. The case originally began in mid-2025 as an individual grievance filed by 23-year-old student Ayesha Jain against Amity University, Noida. Jain alleged that University officials harassed her, barred her from classes and caused her to lose an academic year after she legally changed her name from Khushi Jain to Ayesha Jain. While the Bench pulled up Amity's top officials over their treatment of the student, it refused to close the matter after granting her relief. Instead, in November 2025, Justice Amanullah's Bench expanded the scope of the petition in the larger public interest to scrutinise how private universities across India are established, funded and regulated. When the Union government filed an affidavit through the Higher Education Secretary instead, Justice Amanullah took strong exception , remarking that the Court had shown "magnanimity" by not summoning the Cabinet Secretary to court. items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday allowed eviction proceedings initiated by the Central government against the Delhi Gymkhana Club to continue but restrained the Estate Officer from passing any final order without the Court's prior permission [ Atul Dev & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors. ]. A Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu passed the interim direction while hearing connected appeals arising out of the long-running dispute over the management takeover and land resumption of the historic Lutyens' Delhi club. "Proceedings before the Estate Officer may continue, but no final order may be passed without the permission of this Court," the Bench ordered. It then proceeded to list the matter for final hearing on December 10. Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu The Court was hearing appeals filed by erstwhile members of the club's general committee as well as the Central government challenging different aspects of a judgment rendered by the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) in 2022. The Bench, however, indicated that it was unconvinced by the government's justification for the delay. "They have applied for a recall of the order of this Court whereby the 203-day delay was condoned. We are on this application today. The investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany. For years, Donald Trump’s dealings with Russia have drawn suspicion: What financial interests link him to the country whose president, Vladimir Putin, he has repeatedly heaped with praise? Trump’s former campaign manager, Paul Manafort, was alleged in a U.S. government investigation to have passed on internal campaign information to a man U.S. authorities believe to be linked to the Russian secret service. No evidence has emerged that Trump himself was somehow compromised by his Russian dealings. But now documents from the Inside Deutsche Bank leak show that the global banking institution has long had some potentially critical evidence surrounding Trump, and Russia, in its possession. Leaked files show the bank, whilst processing payments made to some of Trump’s many companies, confirmed in a May 2020 memo that two of those companies were involved in transactions with entities reportedly linked to money-laundering networks or “laundromats” in both Russia and neighbouring Azerbaijan. items.summary: You ask what these contradictions say about solidarity. I will make two points, and then I will say what I think it takes to move beyond visibility and inclusion. Every movement has a default First. Every movement has a default. One group is taken to speak for all. In the anti-racist movement, it was often Black men. In the women’s movement here, it was often dominant-caste Savarna women. In our movement, the anti-caste movement, it is often Dalit men who are cisgender and heterosexual. I say “our” because I am part of this movement. This is not an attack. It is a question we must ask ourselves. Anxiety bigger than pride Twenty-two years ago, with the invitation and support of NCDHR, I went to the World Social Forum in Mumbai in 2004. Some of my queer friends were also holding a pride walk there. I am Dalit, and I am queer. But I knew no open queer person in a Dalit group, and no open Dalit person in a queer group at the time. At the walk, I took a small pride flag and held it in front of my face. The flag was the size of a handkerchief. It did not really cover me. My anxiety was bigger than the flag. I was afraid someone from NCDHR might see me at the pride walk, and that might rupture my relationship with them. No one ever said that to my face. items.title: In the name of women's rights, a plea seeks to limit transgender persons’ rights
items.summary: What does it mean to invoke women's rights to deny an already marginalised community the right to its identity, dignity, and recognition? A petition filed in the Supreme Court by a self-described feminist organisation, Women's Declaration International India (WDI India), has put that question at the centre of a contentious legal battle over transgender rights in India. Arguing that recognising transgender women as women threatens the rights, safety, and entitlements of cisgender women, the organisation wants the Supreme Court to reconsider its landmark 2014 judgment in National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) vs Union of India, which established the constitutional right to legal recognition of gender identity. It also seeks to strike down provisions of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, that enable transgender people to obtain official documents reflecting their gender identity. While WDI India claims that it is not questioning transgender people's right to identify as they wish or their right to protection against discrimination, the reliefs it seeks go considerably further. Among other things, it wants the legal framework enabling transgender persons to obtain documents reflecting their gender identity declared unconstitutional. It also challenges a provision that criminalises verbal and emotional abuse of transgender persons, arguing that it could restrict speech by women advocating for sex-based rights. The petition was filed on October 8, 2026, under Article 32 of the Constitution. On October 28, a Supreme Court Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notice to the Union government and tagged the petition with the ongoing batch of cases challenging the 2026 amendments to the Transgender Persons Act. The central argument raised in the petition is that gender identity and biological sex are distinct, and that recognising someone as a woman on the basis of their gender identity should not automatically entitle them to every protection or benefit specifically intended for women. It argues that the legal framework has allowed people assigned male at birth to obtain documents identifying them as female, and that this undermines women's reservations, employment opportunities, privacy, safety, and access to sex-segregated spaces. items.title: Inside Deutsche Bank: Secrets, scandals and double standards of global financial giant exposed by leak
items.summary: The Inside Deutsche Bank leak was obtained by Indian author and journalist, Josy Joseph, and South African investigative journalist, Khadija Sharife. The Inside Deutsche Bank investigation was coordinated by Barracuda Media in South Africa, with technical support from the Data and Research Center (DARC) in Germany. More than 15 million internal files. Emails from senior executives. Secret risk assessments. Suspicious transaction reports. Private information about billionaires, oligarchs, politicians and royalty. Records involving Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein and sanctioned businessmen. Previously undisclosed companies linked to authoritarian regimes. Together, they add up to the largest cache of internal documents ever leaked to journalists from within a bank. For months, more than 200 reporters from around the world examined the huge cache as part of an investigation called Inside Deutsche Bank. The records span some of the bank’s most sensitive functions and activities: anti-financial crime, sanctions monitoring, internal auditing and the units responsible for deciding whether risky clients stay or go. When Christian Sewing became the chief executive of Deutsche Bank in 2018, after a string of scandals had tainted the bank’s reputation, he promised that the institution would be different: more stable and “a bit more boring.” The bank has since spent years trying to convince the world that its era of scandals is over. The Inside Deutsche Bank project severely tests that narrative, laying bare a bank that built an enormous compliance machinery but repeatedly struggled to make it work. The leak, provided via two whistleblowers, was shared with Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife. Barracuda Media, a non-profit vehicle, was established to analyze the data and share it with reporters from more than 50 global media outlets spanning over 50 countries.
